record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How can secure aggregation tolerate stragglers and dropouts more gracefully, for example through asynchronous variants or aggregation across multiple rounds, and what general-purpose debugging methods can diagnose federated data-pipeline failures without directly inspecting raw user data?

evidence.quote: Another possibility would be to develop an asynchronous version of SecAgg that does not require clients to participate during a ﬁxed window of time ... More speculatively, it may be possible to perform versions of SecAgg that aggregate over multiple computation rounds. ... Developing general-purpose debugging methods for machine learning that do not directly inspect raw data remains a challenge.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central server seeks to compute, in each round, the sum (or average) of model updates contributed by a large population of clients, while ensuring that no individual client's update is revealed to the server or to other clients. A secure aggregation protocol (SecAgg) is a cryptographic protocol that allows the server to learn only the aggregate of the clients' vectors, using pairwise masks (e.g., based on Diffie–Hellman key agreement and secret sharing) that cancel when summed. In standard SecAgg, all participating clients must remain online and respond within a fixed time window of a single synchronous round; clients who are slow ("stragglers") or who disconnect ("dropouts") force the protocol either to wait, to abort, or to reconstruct shared secrets, which scales poorly and limits robustness.

Address the following two open design questions:

(1) Design a secure aggregation protocol that tolerates stragglers and dropouts more gracefully than synchronous SecAgg. Concretely, either:
   (a) construct an asynchronous variant of SecAgg in which clients are not required to participate during a single fixed time window, while still guaranteeing that the server learns only the aggregate of contributed updates and nothing about individual updates; or
   (b) construct a SecAgg variant that aggregates client contributions across multiple computation rounds (so that masks introduced in one round can be canceled by contributions in later rounds), with formal privacy and correctness guarantees against a specified threat model that includes a curious server and a bounded fraction of colluding or dropping clients.
Specify the communication, computation, and round complexity, and prove privacy guarantees that remain meaningful under arbitrary client dropout patterns.

(2) Design general-purpose debugging methods for machine learning training pipelines in the federated setting that can diagnose data-pipeline failures (e.g., malformed features, label corruption, distribution shift, preprocessing bugs) without the debugger or server ever directly inspecting raw user data on individual devices. Formalize what diagnostic information may be released, prove that the released information satisfies a stated privacy notion (e.g., differential privacy or secure aggregation–based release), and demonstrate that the method suffices to localize a class of realistic pipeline bugs.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has made substantial progress on the secure-aggregation portion of the question. Buffered asynchronous secure aggregation protocols such as FedBuff (with TEE-based buffering), BASecAgg (which designs masks that cancel across different rounds without TEEs), Owl, and Buffalo all address stragglers and dropouts in asynchronous or multi-round settings, indicating that the SecAgg-resilience question is partially resolved with multiple constructions, though no single protocol is universally optimal. The privacy-preserving general-purpose debugging question for federated data pipelines remains largely open, with no comprehensive solution established.

status_evidence.title: Secure Aggregation for Buffered Asynchronous Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: BASecAgg addresses this challenge by carefully designing the masks such that they cancel out even if they correspond to different rounds.
status_evidence.claim: An asynchronous, multi-round SecAgg variant (BASecAgg) has been proposed that tolerates stragglers without trusted hardware.

status_evidence.title: Buffalo: A Practical Secure Aggregation Protocol for Buffered Asynchronous FL
status_evidence.snippet: Buffalo: A Practical Secure Aggregation Protocol for Buffered asynchronous federated learning.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2025) work continues to refine practical buffered asynchronous SecAgg, indicating the area is active and partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Let Them Drop: Scalable Federated Learning Solutions Agnostic to Stragglers
status_evidence.snippet: Scalable and Efficient Federated Learning Solutions Agnostic to Stragglers.
status_evidence.claim: Straggler-agnostic SecAgg constructions have been published.
